sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Jowangshin** (*jowangshin*) ​— Kitchen, ‌Hearth · ‌Kitchen king ​spirit — ​belongs to ​the Korean ​tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ​"Kitchen, Hearth". ‌The name ​means "Kitchen ‌king spirit"[^1].

​**Jowangshin** is ‌the kitchen ​king spirit ​who protects the ​hearth, supervises ​the preparation ​of food, ‌and reports ​on the ‌household to ​heaven in ‌Korean tradition. ​The name ‌means "Kitchen ​king spirit" ‌and belongs ​to the ​domain "Kitchen, ‌Hearth." Jowangshin ‌is the ‌spirit of the ​kitchen hearth, ​one of ‌the most ​important household ​deities in ‌Korean folk ​religion. The ​figure is ‌believed to ​record the ‌affairs of ​the household ​and report ​them to ​heaven, so ‌housewives observed ‌taboos such ​as not cursing ‌in the ​kitchen and ​keeping the ‌hearth clean.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Jowangshin** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/jowangshin/). The ​restoration needs ‌no distinctive ​letters or ​diacritics its ​ASCII form ‌would lose, which ​places the ​name in ​Tier 2. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*jowangshin* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ‌domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: National Folk Museum of Korea, Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015).
Kendall, Laurel, Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits (University of Hawaii Press, 1985).
Walraven, Boudewijn, Songs of the Shaman: The Ritual Chants of the Korean Mudang (Kegan Paul International, 1994).

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Hangul ​+ Hanja ​as ​**조왕신 (竈王神)**. ​Etymologically it ​means ‌"Kitchen king ​spirit"[^1].

The ​ASCII ‌form *jowangshin* ​survives ‌only because ​the early ‌domain-name ​system could ​not carry ​diacritics; ​it is ​a ‌technological compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Jowangshin** ‌recovers the ​full ‌diacritic detail ​of the ​scholarly ‌transliteration directly ‌in the ‌address ​bar. The ​restoration ‌needs no ​distinctive letters ​or ‌diacritics its ​ASCII form ​would ‌lose, which ​places ‌the name ​in Tier ​2.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

‌- ‌**j** → ​**J** ‌— Same, ​capitalized
- ​**o** ‌→ **o** ‌— Same
‌- ‌**w** → ​**w** ‌— Same
​- **a** ​→ ​**a** — ‌Same
- ​**n** ​→ **n** ​— ‌Same
- ​**g** → ​**g** ​— Same
‌- **s** ​→ ‌**s** — ​Same
‌- **h** ​→ **h** ‌— ‌Same
- ​**i** → ​**i** ​— Same
​- ‌**n** → ‌**n** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/tɕo.waŋ.ʃin/** ​— Korean ​Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**tɕo** ​— The ​first syllable ‌of ​Jowangshin, carrying ‌primary stress ​in ‌the romanised ​form.
- ​**waŋ** ​— The ​middle syllable ​or ‌element, pronounced ​with level ‌pitch ​in Korean.
‌- **ʃin** ​— ‌The final ​syllable, often ‌closing ​in a ​nasal or ‌simple ‌vowel in ‌the Korean ​reading.

​For the ‌modern speaker, ​the ​closest approximation ‌is: 'joh-WAHNG-sheen' ​— ​The first ‌consonant is ​an unaspirated ‌affricate; ​the second ​syllable carries ​the ​Sino-Korean word ‌for king. ‌The ​name designates ‌the spirit ​who ​rules the ‌kitchen hearth.

‌Kindred ‌and historical ‌forms of ​the ‌name:

- ​**Hangul** — ​조왕신 ​— the ‌Korean script ​form.
​- **Hanja** ​— 竈王神 ‌— ​the Sino-Korean ​character form.

​The ‌first consonant ​is an ‌unaspirated ​affricate; the ‌second syllable ​carries ‌the Sino-Korean ‌word for ​king. ​The name ​designates the ​spirit ‌who rules ‌the kitchen ​hearth.

sources.citation: National Folk Museum of Korea, Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015).

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is preserved ‌in ​Hangul ​+ Hanja ​as ​**조왕신 ​(竈王神)** — ‌Korean ​alphabet ​+ Chinese ‌characters, ​attested ‌Modern Korean, ​in ‌Korea. ​The script ​is ​written ​left-to-right.[^1]

The ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​is ‌*Jowangsin* (Revised ​Romanization), ‌giving ​the normalized ‌reading ​/dʑo.waŋ.ɕin/.

‌The rendering ​proceeds ​step ‌by step:

‌- ‌Hangul ​조왕신 with ​Hanja ‌竈王神 ​— the ​hearth ‌and ​kitchen goddess

​Korean ‌names ​may ‌be written ​in ​Hangul, ​the indigenous ​Korean ‌alphabet, ‌and sometimes ​in ‌Hanja, ​the Sino-Korean ​character ‌set. ‌For **Jowangshin**, ‌the ‌Hangul ​form is ‌**조왕신** ​and ​the Hanja ​form ‌is ​**竈王神**. ​Hangul ‘조왕신’ ​and ‌Hanja ​‘竈王神’; the ​figure ​is ‌also written ​Jowangsin. ‌The ​ASCII form ‌*jowangshin* ​is ‌a technological ‌compromise; ​the ​capitalised restoration ​**Jowangshin** ​is ‌the scholarly ‌citation ​form.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Jowangshin** ​is the ‌kitchen king ‌spirit who ​protects ​the hearth, ​supervises the ​preparation of ​food, ‌and reports ​on the ​household to ‌heaven ​in Korean ‌tradition. The ​name means ‌"Kitchen ​king spirit" ​and belongs ​to the ​domain ​"Kitchen, Hearth." ‌Jowangshin is ​the spirit ‌of ​the kitchen ‌hearth, one ​of the ‌most ​important household ‌deities in ​Korean folk ​religion. ‌The figure ‌is believed ‌to record ​the ​affairs of ‌the household ​and report ​them ‌to heaven, ​so housewives ​observed taboos ‌such ​as not ‌cursing in ​the kitchen ​and ​keeping the ​hearth clean.[^1]

‌### Kitchen ‌King ​Spirit

Jowangshin ‌rules the ​hearth as ​a ‌sovereign deity ‌of the ‌domestic realm.

‌### ​Hearth Fire

‌The fire ​is both ​a ​practical tool ‌and a ​sacred presence ​that ​must be ‌honoured.

### ​Five Taboos

​Rules ​of conduct ‌in the ​kitchen protect ‌the ​household from ‌spiritual and ​practical harm.

‌### ‌Heavenly Report

​The spirit ​records household ​affairs ​and reports ‌them to ‌the celestial ​authorities.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The mythology ​of Jowangshin ‌is preserved ‌in Korean ​oral tradition, ​shamanic ritual ​texts, and ​classical sources ​such as the ‌Samguk Yusa. ​The narratives ​are not ‌merely stories; ​they encode ‌social values, ​ritual obligations, ‌and relationships between ​humans, nature, ​and the ​sacred. Some ​details vary ​by region ‌and by ​shamanic lineage.[^1]

‌### The Munjeon ​Bonpuri (Jeju ‌origin)

In ​the Jeju ‌epic Munjeon ​Bonpuri, the ‌heroine Yeosan ​Buin suffers ​unjust death and ‌is revived ‌by her ‌sons. She ​is appointed ​by Cheonjiwang ‌as Jowangshin, ​the hearth ​goddess who dwells ‌in every ​kitchen and ​reports on ‌family conduct.[^2]

​### The ‌Five Taboos ​(Household cult)

​Traditional households observed ​five rules ​in the ‌kitchen: do ‌not curse, ​do not ‌sit on ​the hearth, ​do not place ‌feet on ‌the hearth, ‌keep the ‌kitchen clean, ​and avoid ‌disrespect to ​the fire. ​Breaking these rules ​risked misfortune.

‌### Sending ​the Report ​to Heaven ​(Annual rite)

‌At the ​end of ​the lunar year ​families performed ‌a rite ​to send ‌Jowangshin to ​heaven with ‌a favourable ​report. Sticky ‌foods such as ‌malt taffy ​were offered ​in the ​hope that ​the spirit's ‌lips would ‌be sealed ​by sweetness.

sources.citation: Kendall, Laurel, Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits (University of Hawaii Press, 1985).
Walraven, Boudewijn, Songs of the Shaman: The Ritual Chants of the Korean Mudang (Kegan Paul International, 1994).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Jowangshin ​is ‌closely ‌parallel to ​the ​Chinese ​Zao ​Jun ​(Kitchen ‌God), and ​the ​two ‌figures ​probably ‌influenced ​each other ‌through ​Sino-Korean ​cultural ​exchange. ​Yet ​the Korean ‌figure ​has ‌its ​own ‌origin epic, ​the ‌Munjeon ​Bonpuri, ‌and ​is ​embedded in ‌distinct ‌shamanic ‌ritual. ​Confucian ​households ‌domesticated the ​cult ​by ‌assigning ​it ​to ‌women's observance, ​while ‌Buddhist ​temples ​sometimes ​honoured ​the hearth ‌spirit ‌as ​a ‌protector. ​Today ​Jowangshin survives ‌in ‌household ‌customs, ‌year-end ​rituals, ‌and the ​lingering ​sense ​that ‌the ​kitchen is ​the ​moral ‌centre ​of ​the ​home.[^1]

Within ‌the ​Korean ‌tradition, ​closely ‌related ​names in ‌the ‌corpus ​include ​[[baekdusan|Baekdusan]], ​[[chilsong|Chilsong]], ​[[dangun|Dangun]], [[halmoni|Halmoni]], ‌[[hananim|Hwanin]], ‌and ​[[hwanung|Hwanung]].

sources.citation: National Folk Museum of Korea, Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015).

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is yet ​assigned ​to ‌Jowangshin ​with ‌certainty. ​That absence ‌should ​be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a Korean ‌name ​of ‌this ​type ‌the material ​record ‌is ​expected ‌to ​be ​thin, and ‌the ‌primary ‌evidence ​remains ​the ‌textual testimony ​gathered ​in ‌the ​Scholarly ​Sources ‌section[^1].

Were ​such ‌evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ​would take ‌recognizable ‌forms: ​votive ‌or ​dedicatory ​inscriptions naming ‌조왕신 ‌(竈王神), ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains tied ​to ​kitchen ​and ‌iconography ​matching its ​traditional ​attributes ‌(hearth ​fire ​and ​cooking pot). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.
